To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

reperfusion of ischemia in sheep lower limbs results in pulmonary microvascular injury, which is not due to increased pulmonary capillary pressure, but is due to a thromboxane-mediated pulmonary hypertension.
lower torso ischemia followed by reperfusion increases pulmonary microvascular leakage in sheep.
reperfusion of ischemia increases pulmonary microvascular leakage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of lower torso ischemia and the subsequent reperfusion on lung microvascular permeability in an animal model.
the effects of hind limb ischemia and reflow on pulmonary microvascular permeation.
the effects of lower extremity ischemia on the pulmonary microvasculature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reperfusion after 2 hr of hind limb ischemia causes a significant increase in lung lymph flow.
the pulmonary edema is not a result of the ischemia, but is a result of the reperfusion.
hind limb ischemia and reoxygenation results in increased pulmonary vascular permeability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ischemic lower limbs increase pulmonary microvascular permeabililty.
reperfusion of lower limbs results in increased pulmonary capillary permeability and that this is due to the release of TxA2.
lower extremity ischemia and re-perfusion results in increased microvascular permeability and edema in the lung.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulmonary vascular endothelium is very sensitive to the effects of ischemia and reoxygenation.
the lung is not a passive organ in this situation and is not just responding to the changes in the pulmonary arterial pressure.
the lung is a target organ of ischemia and reflow in the lower extremities, and that this is mediated by thromboxane A2.
